books.argument: Athena, as Mentes, spurs Telemachus to confront the suitors and seek news of Odysseus.

scenes.summary: The poet invokes the Muse to tell of Odysseus, the man of many wanderings.
The other Achaeans are home; Odysseus alone is held by Calypso, and Poseidon is away among the Ethiopians.
Zeus opens the divine council, citing Aegisthus's punishment as proof mortals suffer beyond fate through folly.
Athena pleads for Odysseus; Zeus explains Poseidon's wrath over the blinded Cyclops Polyphemus and assents to his return.
Athena proposes sending Hermes to Calypso, then herself leaves Olympus for Ithaca.
Disguised as Mentes, Athena finds the suitors feasting; Telemachus, sad at heart, is first to welcome the stranger.
Telemachus welcomes Mentes indoors, seats her apart from the suitors, offers hospitality; the suitors feast, then Phemius sings.
Telemachus confides his despair over the suitors devouring his house and asks the stranger's identity.
Mentes claims kinship with Odysseus's house, insists Odysseus lives and will return, and remarks on Telemachus's resemblance to his father.
Telemachus doubts his paternity, describes the suitors' siege of his house and Penelope's inability to refuse or accept marriage.
Athena urges Telemachus to call an assembly, confront the suitors, and seek news of his father at Pylos and Sparta.
Telemachus offers a parting gift; Athena declines it and departs from the hall in the form of a bird.
Phemius sings the Achaeans' bitter homecoming; Penelope weeps and asks him to stop, but Telemachus rebukes her.
Telemachus announces an assembly at dawn to expel the suitors; Antinous and Eurymachus mock him and question the stranger's identity.
The suitors dance and feast until evening, then depart; Telemachus retires, pondering the journey Athena has revealed.

books.argument: Telemachus confronts the suitors in assembly, then secretly sails for Pylos with Athena's aid.

scenes.summary: At dawn Telemachus rises, arms himself, and summons the Achaeans to assembly, taking his father's seat.
Aegyptius opens the assembly, the first held since Odysseus departed, and asks who has called it.
Telemachus reveals his grief, denounces the suitors for devouring his house, and breaks his staff in tears.
Antinous blames Penelope, recounting how she wove and unraveled Laertes's shroud to delay remarriage.
Telemachus refuses to expel his mother against her will and repeats his curse on the suitors.
Zeus sends two eagles as an omen; Halitherses interprets it as a sign of Odysseus's return.
Eurymachus scorns the prophecy, threatens Halitherses, and restates the wooers' demand that Penelope remarry.
Telemachus asks the assembly for a ship and crew to seek news of his father.
Mentor rebukes the people's silence before the suitors' outrages; Leocritus mocks him and disbands the assembly.
Telemachus prays alone on the shore; Athena, as Mentor, promises a ship and companions for the voyage.
Telemachus returns home; Antinous mocks him with false friendliness, but he refuses to be swayed.
The suitors mock Telemachus among themselves, speculating he plots murder or poison against them.
Telemachus visits the storeroom and secretly orders Eurycleia to provision his voyage; she begs him not to go.
Eurycleia swears silence; Athena gathers a crew and ship, lulls the suitors to sleep, and Telemachus sails by night.

books.argument: At Pylos, Nestor tells Telemachus of the Achaeans' returns and sends him on to Sparta.

scenes.summary: At dawn the ship reaches Pylos, where the people sacrifice bulls to Poseidon on the shore.
Athena urges Telemachus to question Nestor for the truth about his father; he admits his shyness.
Peisistratus welcomes Telemachus and Mentor, seating them at the feast and sharing the sacrificial meat.
Peisistratus hands Athena the ritual cup; she prays to Poseidon for the Pylians and their safe return.
After the feast, Nestor asks the strangers' business; Telemachus asks what became of his father at Troy.
Nestor recalls the ten years' war, naming the dead—Ajax, Achilles, Patroclus, Antilochus—and praises Odysseus's counsel.
Nestor narrates the Atreidae's quarrel at Troy and the fleet's divided, ill-fated departures for home.
Nestor tells of his own safe voyage home and urges Telemachus to be as bold as Orestes.
Telemachus despairs of avenging himself on the suitors; Athena says even the gods cannot ward off death.
Telemachus asks how Agamemnon died; Nestor tells of Aegisthus's seduction of Clytemnestra and the murder.
Nestor narrates Menelaus's storm-driven wanderings and Orestes's vengeance, and urges Telemachus to visit Sparta.
As night falls, Athena proposes returning to the ship, but Nestor insists on housing his guests.
Athena defers Telemachus's lodging to Nestor, says she will return to the ship, and departs as a sea-eagle.
Awed by the sign, Nestor prays to Athena and leads the company to his palace to feast and sleep.
At dawn Nestor rises, gathers his sons, and orders preparations for a sacrifice to Athena.
The Pylians sacrifice a heifer with gilded horns to Athena, described in full ritual detail.
Polycaste bathes Telemachus; after the feast, Nestor has horses yoked for the journey to Sparta.
Telemachus and Peisistratus drive by chariot, resting overnight at Pherae before pressing on toward Sparta.

books.argument: At Sparta, Menelaus tells Telemachus of Proteus's news of Odysseus, while suitors plot ambush.

scenes.summary: Telemachus and Peisistratus arrive at Sparta during a wedding feast and are welcomed at Menelaus's gate.
The guests are bathed and feasted; Menelaus, admiring their bearing, asks to hear their story.
Telemachus marvels at the palace's wealth; Menelaus tells of his wanderings and grieves most for Odysseus.
Helen enters and, struck by the resemblance, guesses the stranger is Telemachus; Menelaus agrees.
Peisistratus confirms Telemachus's identity and mission; Menelaus laments the home he would have given Odysseus.
All weep together, Peisistratus for Antilochus; Menelaus proposes they resume their tales at supper.
Helen drugs the wine to ease grief, then tells of recognizing the disguised Odysseus as a spy in Troy.
Menelaus recalls the Wooden Horse and Helen's mimicry of the Argive wives' voices; Telemachus asks to retire.
At dawn, Menelaus asks Telemachus the purpose of his visit.
Telemachus explains the suitors are ravaging his house and asks for news of his father.
Menelaus recounts being becalmed off Egypt, and Eidothea's counsel to seize her father Proteus for the truth.
Following Eidothea's plan, Menelaus and his men ambush and hold fast the shape-shifting Proteus.
Proteus tells Menelaus that Ajax drowned, killed by Poseidon's wrath at the rock of Gyrae.
Proteus tells of Agamemnon's murder by Aegisthus upon his return home from Troy.
Proteus reveals Odysseus is held weeping on Calypso's isle, and foretells Menelaus's own passage to Elysium.
Menelaus completes his rites in Egypt, sails home, and now offers Telemachus a silver mixing bowl.
At Ithaca, Noemon tells Antinous that Telemachus has sailed to Pylos; Antinous plots an ambush.
Medon warns Penelope that the suitors plan to kill her son; she is overcome with grief.
Penelope grieves and prays to Athena; Eurycleia admits she helped Telemachus depart in secret.
The suitors set an ambush at Asteris; Penelope, fasting, sleeps, and Athena sends a phantom to reassure her.

books.argument: Freed by Zeus's decree, Odysseus leaves Calypso, survives Poseidon's storm, and swims ashore at Scheria.

scenes.summary: At a second divine council, Athena pleads for Odysseus; Zeus sends Hermes to order Calypso to release him.
Hermes flies to Calypso's island, marveling at its beauty, and enters her cave.
Calypso protests the gods' jealousy of goddesses who love mortals, but agrees to release Odysseus.
Calypso finds Odysseus weeping on the shore; wary of a trick, he makes her swear an oath.
Calypso swears the oath; they dine together, and though she urges him to stay, he insists on going home.
At dawn, Calypso gives Odysseus tools and shows him timber; over four days he builds a raft.
On the fifth day Calypso sends Odysseus off with a fair wind; he sails seventeen days by the stars.
On the eighteenth day, Poseidon, returning from the Ethiopians, spots Odysseus and, enraged, raises a storm.
The storm wrecks Odysseus's raft; he nearly drowns and clings to the floating wreckage.
The sea goddess Ino gives Odysseus her magic veil and tells him to abandon the raft and swim ashore.
Poseidon shatters the raft entirely; Odysseus straps on the veil and swims as Athena calms the winds.
For two days and nights Odysseus is tossed at sea; on the third he sights land but finds no harbor.
Driven against the rocks, Odysseus is battered and torn as he struggles to reach the shore.
Athena guides Odysseus to a river mouth; he prays to the river god, lands, and collapses from exhaustion.
Odysseus shelters beneath two intertwined bushes, makes a bed of leaves, and Athena grants him sleep.
scenes.location: a wood near the river, Scheria

books.argument: Nausicaa finds Odysseus on the shore of Scheria and directs him toward the Phaeacian palace.

scenes.summary: Athena travels to the Phaeacian city and enters the chamber where Nausicaa sleeps.
In a dream, disguised as a friend, Athena urges Nausicaa to wash her wedding linens at dawn.
At dawn, Nausicaa asks her father Alcinous for a wagon, concealing her true reason of marriage.
The wagon is loaded with clothes and provisions; Nausicaa drives with her handmaids to the river.
The maidens wash the garments, bathe, dine on the riverbank, and then play ball on the shore.
Athena causes the ball to splash into the water; the maidens' cry wakes Odysseus from sleep.
Naked and shielded by a branch, Odysseus approaches; the maidens flee, but Nausicaa alone stands firm.
Odysseus supplicates Nausicaa, likening her to Artemis and a young palm tree, and begs for help.
Nausicaa reassures her fleeing maidens and orders them to feed, clothe, and bathe the stranger.
Odysseus bathes alone in the river; Athena makes him taller and radiant with grace.
Struck by his transformed looks, Nausicaa wishes aloud for such a husband, then has him fed.
Nausicaa tells Odysseus to follow at a distance to avoid gossip and describes the city and her father's house.
scenes.location: the road to the city, Scheria

scenes.summary: She instructs him to wait in Athena's grove, then enter the palace and supplicate her mother Arete.
scenes.location: the road to the city, Scheria

scenes.summary: At sunset they reach the grove; Odysseus prays to Athena, who hears but withholds her presence, wary of Poseidon.

books.argument: Athena guides Odysseus in mist to the palace of Alcinous, where he is welcomed.
where: the road to the Phaeacian city

scenes.summary: Nausicaa returns to the palace with the mules and raiment; her brothers unyoke the wagon.
Athena shrouds Odysseus in mist, and he sets out for the Phaeacian city.
A girl, Athena in disguise, meets Odysseus, warns of Phaeacian wariness toward strangers, and offers to guide him.
Athena recounts Arete's lineage from Poseidon and Nausithous, urges Odysseus to win her favor, then departs for Athens.
Odysseus marvels at the palace's bronze walls, gold and silver watchdogs, golden torchbearers, orchard, and springs.
Cloaked in mist, Odysseus enters the hall and approaches Arete and Alcinous at their feast.
The mist lifts; Odysseus clasps Arete's knees in supplication, and the hall falls silent in wonder.
Echeneus urges hospitality; Alcinous seats Odysseus, orders wine and food, and plans an assembly and ship for dawn.
Alcinous prays to Zeus for a safe escort home; the feast continues into the evening.
Odysseus begs to eat despite his grief and asks for an escort home at dawn.
Guests withdraw for the night; alone with Alcinous and Arete, she questions Odysseus about his robe and identity.
Odysseus recounts escaping Calypso's island, the storm that wrecked his raft, and his swim ashore.
Alcinous mildly faults Nausicaa for not escorting Odysseus home herself; Odysseus defends her conduct.
Odysseus prays for safe return; Arete has a bed prepared, and the household retires to rest.

books.argument: The Phaeacians hold games and a feast for Odysseus; Demodocus sings, and Odysseus weeps.
where: the Phaeacian assembly and games ground

scenes.summary: At dawn, Athena disguised as a herald rouses the Phaeacian nobles to the assembly.
Alcinous proposes a ship and fifty-two oarsmen to convey the stranger home, and summons Demodocus.
The crew launches and arms the ship; guests gather at Alcinous's palace, and Demodocus is seated.
Demodocus sings the quarrel of Odysseus and Achilles at Troy; Odysseus weeps unseen beneath his cloak.
Alcinous alone notices Odysseus's grief, quietly halts the song, and proposes athletic games.
The company moves to the games; Phaeacian youths compete in racing, wrestling, jumping, discus, and boxing.
Euryalus taunts Odysseus as no athlete but a trader; Odysseus rebukes him sharply.
Angered, Odysseus hurls the discus far past every mark and boasts of his skill with the bow.
Alcinous smooths the quarrel, praises Phaeacian skill in dance and feasting, and calls for dancers and song.
Youths dance while Demodocus sings of Ares and Aphrodite trapped in Hephaestus's net before the laughing gods.
Halius and Laodamas delight the company with a skilled ball-dance.
Alcinous has each of the twelve chiefs bring Odysseus a gift; Euryalus apologizes with a sword.
The gifts are sealed in a chest; Odysseus bathes, dresses, and Nausicaa bids him farewell.
The feast resumes; at Odysseus's request, Demodocus sings of the wooden horse and the fall of Troy.
Odysseus weeps at the tale like a captive woman mourning her slain husband; Alcinous alone notices.
Alcinous halts the song and asks Odysseus to reveal his name, homeland, and story of his wanderings.

books.argument: Odysseus names himself and recounts the Cicones, the Lotus-eaters, and the blinding of Polyphemus.

scenes.summary: Odysseus praises the joy of feast and song, but agrees to tell of his sorrows.
Odysseus names himself, describes rugged Ithaca, and says nothing is sweeter than one's own land.
At Ismarus the crew sacks the Cicones' city; lingering to feast, they are routed with heavy losses.
A nine-day storm drives the fleet to the Lotus-eaters; scouts who taste the lotus must be forced back aboard.
The fleet reaches an islet off the land of the lawless, shipless Cyclopes.
The crew lands on the isle by night, feasts on wild goats, and eyes the Cyclopes' land.
Odysseus takes one ship and twelve men to the Cyclopes' shore, carrying a skin of potent wine.
The men enter Polyphemus's unattended cave and eat his cheese; he returns and seals the entrance with a boulder.
Polyphemus demands their identity; Odysseus invokes Zeus, protector of strangers, but the Cyclops scorns the gods and seizes two men.
Polyphemus devours two men; Odysseus restrains his urge for immediate revenge, unable to move the sealing stone.
Polyphemus eats two more men and drives his flock out at dawn; alone, Odysseus sharpens a stake.
That evening Polyphemus eats two more men; Odysseus plies him with wine and gives his name as Noman.
Drunk, Polyphemus sleeps; Odysseus and his men drive the heated stake into his single eye, blinding him.
The blinded Cyclops gropes at the cave mouth; Odysseus straps his men beneath rams to slip past unseen.
Reaching the ship, Odysseus taunts Polyphemus from the sea and reveals his true name against his men's pleas.
Enraged, Polyphemus hurls a rock at the ship and prays to Poseidon to curse Odysseus's homecoming.
The crew reunites, sacrifices the ram to Zeus, and sails on grieving, having lost dear comrades.

books.argument: Odysseus recounts Aeolus's winds, the Laestrygonians' slaughter of his fleet, and Circe's island.

scenes.summary: At Aeolia, King Aeolus hosts the crew a month, then gives Odysseus a bag binding the contrary winds.
Nearing Ithaca, Odysseus sleeps; his men, suspecting treasure, open the bag, and the freed winds blow them back to Aeolia.
Aeolus refuses further help, declaring Odysseus hateful to the gods, and sends him away.
At the Laestrygonians' harbor, the giant king and his people crush and spear most of the fleet; one ship escapes.
The survivors reach Aeaea, the island of Circe.
Odysseus kills a great stag alone; the crew feasts and rests two days on the shore.
Odysseus reports smoke rising inland; the crew casts lots, and Eurylochus leads half the men to investigate.
Circe lures Eurylochus's party into her house with drugged food and turns them into swine.
Terrified, Eurylochus alone returns and refuses to guide Odysseus back to Circe's house.
Hermes meets Odysseus, warns him of Circe's magic, and gives him the herb moly for protection.
Circe's drugs fail against Odysseus; he draws his sword, forces an oath of safety, and they become lovers.
Circe's maidens bathe and feast Odysseus, who sits joyless, grieving for his transformed comrades.
At Odysseus's demand, Circe restores the swine to men, younger and fairer than before.
Circe sends Odysseus to fetch the rest of the crew; despite Eurylochus's fear, they return to her house.
Circe kindly welcomes the remaining crew and has them bathed and fed.
Circe urges the still-despondent men to eat, drink, and recover their spirits.
The crew stays a full year feasting; when they ask to leave, Circe says Odysseus must first consult Teiresias.
Circe instructs the rites for summoning the dead: the trench, libations, and sacrifice of a ram and ewe.
As they prepare to leave, the young Elpenor, drunk, falls from Circe's roof and dies.
Circe sends the crew off with provisions and a fair wind toward the house of Hades.

books.argument: Odysseus recounts summoning the dead at world's edge and consulting the seer Teiresias.
where: the edge of Ocean, land of the Cimmerians

scenes.summary: The ship reaches the stream of Ocean and the Cimmerians' land of mist; the crew performs Circe's rites.
Unburied Elpenor's shade appears first and begs Odysseus to return and give him proper burial.
The shade of Odysseus's mother Anticleia appears, but he holds her back until he questions Teiresias.
Teiresias foretells Poseidon's wrath, the peril of the Cattle of the Sun, the suitors' doom, and a gentle death.
Anticleia describes affairs in Ithaca — Penelope's faithfulness, Telemachus, Laertes' grief — and her own death of longing.
A procession of heroines' shades appears: Tyro, Antiope, Alcmena, Epicaste, Chloris, Leda, Phaedra, Ariadne, and others.
The Phaeacians, moved by the tale, urge lavish gifts; Alcinous asks Odysseus to stay and tell more.
Odysseus answers Alcinous's request to stay; Alcinous then asks about the Trojan dead, and Odysseus agrees to continue his tale.
Agamemnon's shade recounts his murder by Aegisthus and Clytemnestra, and warns against trusting women.
Achilles' shade says he would rather serve a poor man alive than rule the dead, but rejoices at his son.
The still-resentful shade of Ajax refuses to speak, still angry over the contest for Achilles' arms.
Odysseus sees Minos judging the dead, Orion hunting, and Tityus, Tantalus, and Sisyphus in eternal torment.
The phantom of Heracles greets Odysseus and recounts his own hard labors.
Fearing the Gorgon's head may rise, Odysseus retreats to his ship and sails from Hades.

books.argument: Odysseus recounts the Sirens, Scylla and Charybdis, and the crew's slaughter of the Sun's cattle.
where: the strait of Scylla and Charybdis

scenes.summary: The crew returns to Circe's isle and gives Elpenor full burial rites, raising a mound and his oar.
Circe welcomes the crew, provisions the ship, and publicly tells them to eat and sail at dawn.
Circe describes the Sirens' song and instructs Odysseus to seal his men's ears and bind himself to the mast.
Circe warns of the Wandering Rocks, passable only once, by the Argo.
Circe describes Scylla's cave and her six heads, each seizing a sailor from passing ships.
Circe describes Charybdis's whirlpool and advises hugging Scylla's cliff, losing six men rather than the ship.
Circe warns that harming the Sun's sacred cattle on Thrinacia dooms both ship and crew.
At dawn Circe departs; Odysseus tells his men only of the Sirens and prepares the wax and bindings.
Nearing the Sirens, the crew's ears are sealed and Odysseus is bound; the Sirens sing, and he begs release.
Past the Sirens, seeing smoke and surf ahead, Odysseus withholds Circe's warning and orders the men to row hard.
Passing between Scylla and Charybdis, Scylla darts out and seizes six men, who cry out as she devours them.
scenes.location: the strait of Scylla and Charybdis

scenes.summary: The survivors reach Thrinacia and hear the lowing of the Sun's cattle.
Odysseus urges sailing past the island, but the exhausted crew, led by Eurylochus, forces a landing.
A month-long storm traps them on the island; food runs low, and the men resort to hunting and fishing.
While Odysseus sleeps, Eurylochus persuades the starving crew to slaughter the Sun's cattle.
Helios demands vengeance from Zeus; the crew feasts on the cattle for days despite ominous portents.
Setting sail, the ship is wrecked by Zeus's thunderbolt; all the crew drown but Odysseus.
Odysseus clings to a fig tree above Charybdis until the wreckage resurfaces, then rafts away.
scenes.location: the strait of Scylla and Charybdis

scenes.summary: Odysseus drifts nine days and reaches Ogygia, Calypso's island, where his tale began.

books.argument: The Phaeacians land Odysseus on Ithaca; Poseidon punishes their ship; Athena reveals him home.

scenes.summary: Alcinous pledges further gifts and the Phaeacian lords retire for the night.
At dawn the Phaeacians load Odysseus's gifts, feast, and sacrifice to Zeus.
At sunset Odysseus bids Alcinous, the assembled lords, and Arete farewell and boards ship.
The Phaeacian ship sails through the night while Odysseus sleeps a deep, deathlike sleep.
At dawn the ship reaches Ithaca's harbor of Phorcys; the crew lay the sleeping Odysseus ashore with his goods.
Poseidon protests to Zeus that Odysseus reached home safely and wins leave to punish the Phaeacian ship.
As the city watches, Poseidon turns the returning Phaeacian ship to stone; Alcinous orders a propitiary sacrifice.
Odysseus wakes on his own shore unrecognizing it beneath Athena's mist; he grieves and counts his treasure.
Disguised as a young shepherd, Athena questions Odysseus, who answers with a false Cretan cover story.
Amused, Athena reveals her true form and outlines her plan to hide his treasure and defeat the suitors.
Still doubting he is home, Odysseus is convinced when Athena dispels the mist; he kisses the earth and prays.
They hide the treasure in the nymphs' cave, plot the suitors' deaths; Athena disguises Odysseus as a beggar.
scenes.location: Ithaca, the cave of the Naiads

books.argument: Disguised Odysseus is welcomed by Eumaeus the swineherd and tells a false tale.

scenes.summary: Odysseus climbs to Eumaeus's remote steading, walled and fenced, with its many sties of swine.
The guard dogs rush Odysseus; Eumaeus drives them off and laments his absent master.
Eumaeus receives the stranger hospitably, seats him on a goatskin, and explains a slave's dutiful piety.
Eumaeus slaughters two pigs for the meal and denounces the suitors' impious plundering of Odysseus's estate.
Testing Eumaeus, Odysseus asks after his master; Eumaeus, wary of lying wanderers, mourns him all the same.
Eumaeus recounts Telemachus's voyage to Pylos and the suitors' ambush, then asks the stranger's own story.
Odysseus invents a Cretan identity: a wealthy man's bastard son, proud in raiding and war.
The false tale continues: Trojan War service, a disastrous raid on Egypt, and mercy from its king.
The tale continues: years in Egypt, betrayal by a Phoenician trader, shipwreck, and a Thesprotian rescue with news of Odysseus.
Eumaeus, moved yet unpersuaded, refuses to believe Odysseus will return, recalling an earlier wanderer's lie.
The herdsmen return with the swine; a boar is sacrificed, and Odysseus is honored with the choicest cut.
In a cold, stormy night Odysseus tells an old ambush anecdote at Troy, hinting for a cloak.
Eumaeus gives him a bed by the fire and goes out armed to guard the swine himself.

books.argument: Athena hastens Telemachus's return from Sparta as Odysseus lingers with Eumaeus, testing him.

scenes.summary: By night at Sparta, Athena warns Telemachus of an ambush and urges him toward Eumaeus first.
At dawn, Telemachus rouses Peisistratus to hasten their departure from Sparta.
Telemachus asks Menelaus to send him home at once; Menelaus orders a parting meal prepared.
Menelaus and Helen bring treasures from the storeroom, choosing a mixing-bowl and an embroidered robe for Telemachus.
A farewell feast is served, and Menelaus formally presents his gifts to Telemachus.
An eagle seizes a goose as the chariot departs; Helen reads it as a sign of Odysseus's vengeful return.
They drive to Pherae, lodge overnight with Diocles, and at dawn resume toward Pylos.
Reaching Pylos, Telemachus persuades Peisistratus to leave him at the ship, avoiding delay with Nestor.
At the ship, Telemachus sacrifices to Athena; the fugitive seer Theoclymenus approaches, fleeing a blood feud.
Telemachus takes Theoclymenus aboard; they sail with a fair wind, coasting past Elis into the night.
At Eumaeus's hut, Odysseus proposes going to town to beg among the suitors.
Eumaeus urges him to wait for Telemachus; Odysseus, still probing, asks after Laertes and Odysseus's mother.
Eumaeus recounts his own history: a chieftain's son kidnapped by a nurse and Phoenician traders, sold into slavery.
The two finally lie down for a brief night's sleep.
At dawn Telemachus's ship reaches Ithaca; he disembarks and sends the ship on to town.
Telemachus entrusts Theoclymenus to Peiraeus, reads a hawk-and-dove omen, and walks toward Eumaeus's farmstead.

books.argument: Telemachus returns to Eumaeus's hut, where Odysseus reveals himself; the suitors plot his death.

scenes.summary: At dawn at the hut, the hounds fawn rather than bark, signaling Telemachus's arrival.
Eumaeus rushes out and embraces Telemachus like a father welcoming home a beloved son.
Telemachus enters, gives the disguised Odysseus his seat, and they share a meal together.
Telemachus, hearing the stranger's story, hesitates to shelter him amid the suitors' danger; the stranger denounces their outrages.
Telemachus explains his family's thin, only-child lineage leaves him without kin to resist the suitors.
Telemachus sends Eumaeus to tell Penelope privately of his return, withholding the news from Laertes.
Eumaeus departs; Athena, unseen by Telemachus, restores Odysseus to his true, youthful form.
Telemachus, disbelieving, takes the transformed man for a god until Odysseus reveals himself as his father.
Odysseus explains the Phaeacians' voyage and the hidden treasure, then asks the suitors' numbers and strength.
Telemachus counts over a hundred suitors; Odysseus proposes trusting Athena and Zeus and outlines his plan for vengeance.
Telemachus's ship reaches Ithaca; the crew stores the gifts and sends word of his return to Penelope.
The alarmed suitors debate; Antinous urges killing Telemachus outright, but Amphinomus persuades them to await a sign from the gods.
Penelope publicly rebukes Antinous for plotting against her son; Eurymachus falsely reassures her while secretly conspiring.
That evening Eumaeus returns; Athena disguises Odysseus again as a beggar before they sup and retire.

books.argument: Telemachus returns to town; Eumaeus leads disguised Odysseus there to beg among the suitors.

scenes.summary: At dawn Telemachus sets off for town, telling Eumaeus to bring the stranger along later.
Odysseus agrees to follow once warmed by the sun, preferring to beg in the town.
At the palace, the household and Penelope greet Telemachus with tears; she presses him for news.
Telemachus meets Theoclymenus and Peiraeus, and brings the seer home rather than risk him among the suitors.
Telemachus and his guest bathe and dine at the palace while Penelope spins nearby.
Penelope questions Telemachus, who relates Nestor's and Menelaus's news that Odysseus is held captive by Calypso.
Theoclymenus prophesies that Odysseus is already in Ithaca, plotting against the suitors.
The suitors sport before their midday meal, while Eumaeus and Odysseus set out for town.
scenes.location: outside the palace / road to town

scenes.summary: On the road the goatherd Melanthius reviles and kicks Odysseus, who restrains his anger.
Eumaeus prays to the local nymphs for his master's return as Melanthius hurries ahead.
Nearing the hall, Eumaeus and Odysseus debate who should enter first.
The aged hound Argos recognizes his master, wags his tail, and dies.
Odysseus sits at the threshold; Telemachus sends him food while the minstrel Phemius sings.
Athena prompts Odysseus to beg from the suitors in turn; Antinous rebukes Eumaeus for bringing him.
Odysseus tells Antinous a false tale of Egypt and Cyprus and asks for alms; Antinous refuses with insults.
Antinous hurls a footstool at Odysseus; the suitors murmur, and Penelope, informed, prays for Antinous's death.
Penelope summons the stranger, but Odysseus, through Eumaeus, asks to wait until evening for safety.
Eumaeus reports back, warns Telemachus to be watchful, and returns to the farm as evening merriment continues.

books.argument: Irus challenges Odysseus and loses; Penelope charms gifts from the suitors that evening.

scenes.summary: The town beggar Irus tries to drive Odysseus from the threshold, and the two exchange threats.
Antinous arranges a boxing match between them, offering a goat's paunch as the prize.
Odysseus strips to reveal a powerful frame, enhanced by Athena, terrifying Irus.
Odysseus fells Irus with a single blow and drags him from the hall.
Amphinomus toasts the victorious stranger with bread and wine.
Odysseus warns Amphinomus of fortune's fragility and urges him to leave before Odysseus returns, though his doom is fixed.
Athena inspires Penelope to appear before the suitors; she debates with Eurynome over grooming herself.
Athena lulls Penelope to sleep and beautifies her with divine gifts.
Veiled, Penelope appears before the suitors and rebukes Telemachus for allowing the stranger's abuse.
Eurymachus flatters her; Penelope recalls Odysseus's parting words and faults the suitors for not courting properly.
Antinous calls for gifts; each suitor sends for treasures, and Penelope withdraws with them.
Odysseus offers to tend the torches; the maid Melantho insults him, and he threatens to report her.
Eurymachus mocks Odysseus's baldness and offers him farm labor; Odysseus retorts, boasting of his old prowess.
Enraged, Eurymachus hurls a stool and misses; Telemachus rebukes the uproar, and the suitors retire for the night.

books.argument: Penelope questions the disguised beggar; Eurycleia recognizes Odysseus by the scar on his leg.

scenes.summary: Guided by Athena's light, Odysseus and Telemachus remove the suitors' weapons from the hall; Eurycleia locks the maids away.
Penelope enters the hall; Melantho again taunts the beggar, and Penelope sharply rebukes her insolence.
Penelope questions the stranger's identity; he praises her fame while she recounts the suitors' pressure and her weaving ruse.
Still unrecognized, Odysseus begins a false tale: a Cretan prince who once hosted Odysseus bound for Troy.
He recounts a storm-delayed voyage and describes Odysseus's cloak-pin and herald as proof; Penelope weeps at the signs.
Odysseus swears an oath that Odysseus lives nearby and will return within the month.
Penelope orders a bath prepared; the beggar asks for an old woman's service, and Eurycleia is summoned.
Eurycleia laments the stranger's likeness to Odysseus; wary of the firelight, he turns his scarred leg into shadow.
Eurycleia washes his feet; the poet recalls how a boar's tusk on Parnassus gave young Odysseus his scar.
Eurycleia recognizes the scar and nearly cries out; Odysseus seizes her throat and swears her to silence.
Eurycleia promises silence and offers to name disloyal maids; Odysseus declines for now and finishes the foot-washing.
Penelope confesses her nightly grief, likened to the mourning nightingale, torn between loyalty and remarriage.
She recounts a dream of an eagle killing twenty geese; the stranger interprets it as Odysseus's certain vengeance.
Unconvinced by the gates of dream, Penelope announces the contest of the bow and axes for the morrow.
Penelope retires weeping to her chamber; Athena at last grants her sleep.

books.argument: Dawn breaks on the festival of Apollo; omens gather as the suitors feast.

scenes.summary: Wakeful in the portico, Odysseus watches disloyal maids slip out to the suitors and burns with rage.
He masters his fury with the image of a dog guarding pups and a boiling paunch, resolved to wait.
Athena appears, promises victory even against many foes, and grants him sleep.
Penelope wakes weeping and prays to Artemis for death rather than a lesser husband, as dawn breaks.
Hearing her, Odysseus prays to Zeus for a sign; Zeus thunders, and a mill-woman's curse on the suitors answers it.
The household wakes; Telemachus orders the hall swept and readied, noting it is the suitors' feast-day.
Servants fetch wood and water; Eumaeus arrives with the choicest pigs for the feast.
Melanthius the goatherd arrives with goats and again reviles Odysseus.
Philoetius the cowherd arrives, laments his absent master, and hears Odysseus swear that Odysseus will return and slay the suitors.
Philoetius and Eumaeus pray for their master's return; an eagle omen and Amphinomus's counsel turn the suitors from killing Telemachus.
The feast begins; Telemachus seats Odysseus with honor; Ctesippus hurls an ox-hoof at him and is sharply rebuked.
Agelaus urges peace and presses Telemachus toward his mother's remarriage; Telemachus insists the choice remains hers.
Athena stirs the suitors to wild, uncontrollable laughter and tears, a portent of coming death.
Theoclymenus sees blood on the walls and the sun blotted out, prophesies doom, and is mocked and driven off.

books.argument: Penelope sets the contest of the bow; alone among all the suitors, Odysseus strings it.

scenes.summary: Athena inspires Penelope to set the contest; the poet recalls the bow as Iphitus's gift-friendship to Odysseus.
Penelope fetches the bow and quiver from the storeroom, weeping over her husband's relic.
She brings the bow before the suitors: whoever strings it and shoots through twelve axes wins her hand.
Eumaeus and the cowherd weep at the sight of the bow; Antinous mocks their tears.
Telemachus sets up the axes and tries the bow three times, yielding it on a silent sign from his father.
Leiodes the seer tries first and fails, warning the bow will cost many suitors their lives.
Antinous rebukes him and has Melanthius warm the bow with fire and grease; more suitors fail in turn.
Odysseus leads the herdsmen outside, reveals his scar, swears them to loyalty, and orders the doors locked.
Eurymachus tries and fails, lamenting the shame such failure brings before later generations.
Antinous proposes deferring the contest until tomorrow's sacrifice to Apollo, over libations.
Odysseus asks to try the bow; the suitors refuse in fear, and Antinous threatens him with exile to King Echetus.
Eurymachus, fearing gossip, urges the bow be given to the stranger; Penelope insists and promises him fine gifts.
Telemachus asserts his authority over the bow and sends his weeping mother upstairs to sleep.
Amid the suitors' jeers, Eumaeus carries the bow to Odysseus; the hall and courtyard doors are locked.
Odysseus strings the bow with ease and shoots clean through all twelve axes as Zeus thunders in confirmation.

books.argument: Odysseus slays the suitors in his own hall, aided by Telemachus, Eumaeus, Philoetius, and Athena.

scenes.summary: Stripping off his rags, Odysseus leaps to the threshold and shoots Antinous through the throat as he lifts a cup.
The suitors, thinking it an accident, threaten the beggar until he declares himself Odysseus, master of the house.
Eurymachus blames the crime on dead Antinous alone and begs Odysseus to spare the suitors' lives.
Odysseus refuses reconciliation and orders them to fight or flee; Eurymachus urges the suitors to draw swords and charge.
Amphinomus charges Odysseus and falls to a spear-thrust from Telemachus.
Telemachus arms the four defenders with fetched shields and spears; Agelaus proposes a side door to raise the town.
Melanthius the goatherd slips through the side door to arm the suitors from Odysseus's own storeroom.
Caught on a second trip, Melanthius is bound by Eumaeus and Philoetius and hoisted to the rafters.
Athena arrives disguised as Mentor; Agelaus threatens her, and, still testing Odysseus, she perches as a swallow on the roof-beam.
Agelaus rallies the suitors' champions to volley together at Odysseus, but Athena turns every spear aside.
The defenders' counter-volley kills four suitors; Athena raises her aegis and routs the rest in panic.
Leiodes the seer clasps Odysseus's knees, pleading his innocence; Odysseus kills him regardless.
Phemius the bard begs for his life; Telemachus intercedes, and the herald Medon, found cowering, is likewise spared.
The last suitors are cut down; Odysseus surveys the dead heaped like fish on a shore.
Telemachus fetches Eurycleia, who finds Odysseus amid the corpses and is checked before she can exult aloud.
Odysseus asks which maidservants dishonored the house; Eurycleia names twelve who consorted with the suitors.
The disloyal maids clean the hall under compulsion and are hanged in the courtyard; Melanthius is mutilated and killed.
Odysseus purifies the hall with fire and sulfur as the loyal maidservants joyfully embrace their returned master.

books.argument: Penelope at last recognizes Odysseus; reunited, they retire, and he departs for Laertes's farm.

scenes.summary: Eurycleia hurries upstairs to wake Penelope: Odysseus has returned and killed the suitors; Penelope doubts her.
Eurycleia insists it is true, revealing that Telemachus knew and kept his father's return secret.
Eurycleia describes finding Odysseus standing among the slain suitors as the house is purified with fire.
Penelope remains unconvinced, suspecting a god punished the suitors' outrages rather than Odysseus himself.
Penelope goes down to the hall, uncertain whether to embrace the stranger or question him from apart.
Telemachus rebukes his mother's coldness; she says only private, hidden tokens can prove this is truly Odysseus.
Odysseus, smiling, tells Telemachus to let her test him, then turns to plan concealing the slaughter from the town.
A mock wedding-feast of music and dancing is staged to deceive passersby into thinking no violence occurred.
Eurynome bathes Odysseus, and Athena makes him taller and more radiant; he returns to sit before the still-unmoved Penelope.
Odysseus reproaches her hard heart; testing him further, Penelope orders their bridal bed moved outside the chamber.
Stung, Odysseus describes how he built the bed himself around a living olive tree rooted in the ground.
Penelope's knees give way at the proof; she runs to him in tears, asking pardon for her caution.
Husband and wife weep together as Athena prolongs the night, holding back the dawn.
Odysseus warns his trials are not over, recounting Teiresias's prophecy of a journey inland bearing an oar.
The marriage bed is prepared, and the reunited couple retires to it at last.
Before sleep, they exchange full accounts of their sufferings: Penelope's ordeal with the suitors, Odysseus's wanderings.
At last Athena releases the dawn; Odysseus arms himself and his men and departs for Laertes's farm, veiled in mist.

books.argument: The suitors' shades reach Hades; Odysseus reveals himself to Laertes; Athena secures peace on Ithaca.

scenes.summary: Hermes leads the shrieking suitors' shades to the underworld meadow, where Achilles' and Agamemnon's shades meet one another.
Agamemnon recalls Achilles' glorious funeral at Troy, contrasting it with his own squalid murder at home.
The suitors' shades arrive; Agamemnon recognizes Amphimedon, a former host, and asks how so many nobles died.
Amphimedon narrates Penelope's weaving trick and Odysseus's disguised return and slaughter of the suitors.
Agamemnon praises Penelope's faithfulness, contrasting it with Clytemnestra's infamous treachery.
Odysseus reaches Laertes's farm, finds his father alone in shabby clothes tending the vines, and resolves to test him first.
Odysseus mocks the old man's neglected appearance; weeping, Laertes describes suitor-ruled Ithaca and asks after the guest he once hosted.
Odysseus spins a final false tale as 'Eperitus,' then, moved by his father's grief, embraces and reveals himself.
Laertes demands proof; Odysseus shows the boar-scar and names the orchard trees given him as a boy.
They set out for the farmhouse; bathed and touched by Athena, Laertes stands taller, to Telemachus's wonder.
Dolius and his sons arrive, recognize Odysseus with joy, and the household dines together.
News of the slaughter spreads through the town; the grieving assembly hears Eupeithes, mourning Antinous, call for vengeance.
Medon and Phemius warn that a god fought beside Odysseus; Halitherses counsels peace, blaming the suitors' own folly.
The assembly splits; half stay behind while the rest arm under Eupeithes and march on Laertes's farm.
Athena asks Zeus's intent for Ithaca; he grants Odysseus's rule and decrees a lasting peace, sending her to enforce it.
The armed townsmen attack; Laertes kills Eupeithes, and Athena halts the battle as Zeus's thunderbolt seals a lasting peace.
